rationale: The Egyptian invasion force includes Libyans and Ethiopians; the later prophetic rebuke also names Ethiopians and Libyans as a great force. These are different campaigns, and the source's horses and chariot counts are not transferred to Asa's battle.

The stolen gold shields are attributed to Solomon, whose earlier manufacture of large hammered-gold shields and an additional set of gold shields is recorded. The connection traces the royal gold armament without asserting that every described shield was carried off individually.

Abijah opens his address by calling Jeroboam and Israel to listen; its concluding warning again addresses Israel's sons and declares that fighting the Lord will not prosper. These units mark the speech's audience and appeal.

Terror from the Lord comes upon the communities around Gedor during Asa's victory; the later account reports such terror among all the kingdoms of the earth after hearing the Lord fought Israel's adversaries. The different geographical extents remain distinct.

relationship: Royal cult-removal comparison with differing details
rationale: Both place Asa's removal of his mother beside destruction by fire at the Kedron or Kidron watercourse. Chronicles names Maacah, ministry to Astarte, and an idol; Kings names Ana, leadership, a grove gathering, and her hiding places. This narrative comparison does not resolve the woman's identity or equate the differently described objects.

Both report Asa bringing in silver, gold, and vessels. Chronicles describes holy things of David and of the Lord God's house; Kings explicitly gives the Lord's house as the destination and calls the objects his father's and his own pillars. The distinct object descriptions and wording about the house remain intact.

The Lord's eyes examining the earth to strengthen whole hearts corresponds to David's charge that the Lord examines every heart and should be served with a whole heart. Chronicles places this assurance of strength within the rebuke about Asa's reliance and coming war.

Jehoshaphat seeks the Lord and walks in his father's commandments. Asa had expressly instructed Judah to seek the Lord and carry out the law and commandments, providing a concrete earlier paternal instruction corresponding to this conduct.

Both Jehoshaphat passages connect terror from the Lord with freedom from attack or rest. The source specifies kingdoms around Judah; the later passage says all the kingdoms of the earth and explains their terror by hearing of divine victory, a cause not stated in this source unit.

The report of gifts from foreigners and livestock from Arabs extends the earlier notice of gifts from all Judah. The distinction between domestic and foreign gifts clarifies the narrative's picture of prosperity without identifying the foreign groups more narrowly.

The roster gives Ednas 300,000 men from Judah, matching the numerical total of Asa's earlier Judah force. The kings and occasions differ, and the earlier unit names no commander; an identical military unit or unchanged force is not claimed.
